transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Start: 15:00 PT | Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Laura (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Aisha (CTO), Mark (Head of ML), Jing (Infra)
---
[00:00] Laura: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Laura from Redwood, AE on the account. Samir is our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Aisha: Good, thanks. Sorry for the slight delay, flights.
[00:15] Mark: Hey all. Ready to dig in.
[00:20] Samir: Awesome. I'll share a quick agenda - qualification, current infra, workload, dedicated capacity options, then discuss security/isolation and next steps. Sound good?
[00:30] Aisha: Yeah. We're primarily evaluating dedicated vs hosted vs private, but dedicated is top of list because of isolation and cost predictability.
[01:12] Samir: Great - can you give us a quick picture of current usage and the product lines using LLMs?
[01:25] Mark: Sure. We're a fintech - real-time risk scoring, transaction enrichment, a support agent for internal ops. Most of our models are open weights fine-tuned in-house. Right now everything runs in our AWS account on EC2 with some Kubernetes. Latency target for risk scoring is sub-200ms p50 and p95 ideally under 500ms. Throughput average is ~120 qps during business hours but spikes to 800 qps for short windows. Sequence lengths vary: short prompts mostly 64-128 tokens, the enrichment pipeline can hit 512 occasionally.
[02:05] Jing: Infra concerns: we need VPC isolation, control over key material, and audit logs sent to our SIEM. SOC2 is mandatory, and we do quarterly audits. We'll also need contract language about data residency (US-only).
[02:22] Laura: That's helpful. Our Dedicated offering supports reserved GPU pools in a VPC with customer-managed networking and KMS integrations. For SOC2 we can share our attestation artifacts, and for data residency we can pin regions.
[02:45] Mark: Cool. Two questions off the top: 1) how do you handle burst spikes - we can't overprovision for 800 qps if it's only occasional, and 2) what's the expected cost delta between hosted pay-as-you-go vs a committed dedicated cluster?
[03:10] Samir: For bursts we have a few levers: burst capacity options on Dedicated (short-term overcommit), autoscaling policies tuned for queueing and cold-starts, and fast fallback to a smaller hosted pool if needed. The economics depend on model size and token counts. Roughly, customers see 30-60% lower per-token unit cost on Dedicated with reasonable commitments versus hosted. We'll give concrete pricing once we see your token profile.
[04:00] Aisha: About the fallback - if we route to hosted during bursts, does that leak data out of our VPC or break compliance?
[04:18] Laura: Good question. We can set policies so only anonymized or non-sensitive routes can fallback; otherwise we can allow burst only within the private/dedicated footprint. For regulated flows, many customers choose cold standby instances in the same VPC or use an on-prem option. We'll document options.
[04:40] Mark: What's the onboarding look like for Dedicated? We want minimal engineering lift.
[04:50] Samir: Typical onboarding: capacity planning call, pilot dedicated cluster (2-4 weeks), benchmark runs, then commit and schedule capacity reservation. We provide deployment templates (Terraform/Helm), RBAC mappings, and a private control plane option if you want us to operate without sending PII to our hosted control plane.
[05:30] Jing: Can you talk about key management? We use AWS KMS and an external HSM for high-value keys.
[05:40] Samir: We integrate with customer KMS - bring-your-own-key. For HSM-backed keys we have vendor integrations and can support TLS mutual auth between infra components. We'll share a diagram.
[06:10] Aisha: On models: we fine-tune open models; how does Redwood handle quantized weights and model variants? We often run 13B-33B families and sometimes 70B for overnight batch.
[06:30] Samir: The runtime supports mixed precision, quantization-friendly execution, and kernel selection based on model architecture. For 13B/33B we can run more instances per GPU with int8/4 quantization; 70B may require bfloat16 and bigger GPUs. We also support model pinning and automatic fallback to compatible variants.
[07:05] Mark: Latency - you mentioned kernel selection. What kind of p50/p95 should we expect for a 33B with 128 tokens on an A100-like GPU?
[07:20] Samir: Ballpark: p50 ~80-120ms, p95 under 350ms depending on batching and KV cache hit rates. If you need consistent sub-200 p95 we often suggest smaller sequence budgets, KV caching of prefixes, and dedicated inference nodes per latency-critical route. We'll run benchmarks to confirm for your prompt mix.
[08:00] Aisha: We also have multitenant safety concerns - we can't have noisy neighborism. How isolated are the GPU pools?
[08:15] Laura: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools - those GPUs are not shared with other customers. You can choose strict tenancy with node-level isolation. For higher security, we offer private deployments where the control plane is in your VPC/on-prem.
[08:40] Jing: Do you support multi-AZ within a region for HA?
[08:48] Samir: Yes, Dedicated clusters can span AZs, with replication for model state and warm standby nodes. The control plane orchestrates failover; we provide SLOs for uptime in the contract.
[09:15] Mark: Cost structure: curious about commitment shapes - monthly vs annual vs usage credits? Also any overage pricing?
[09:30] Laura: We have monthly and annual reserved capacity. Commitments give you discounted rates and burst credits. Overage is charged at a higher committed rate; there are also options for auto-scaled burst pools billed separately. We'll include templates in the deck.
[10:05] Aisha: For our security/compliance folks, can we get SOC2 and architecture docs before internal sign-off?
[10:12] Laura: Yes - Samir will send SOC2 and whitepapers after the call.
[10:20] Samir: I'll also include a sample network diagram showing VPC peering, NAT, and where logs go to your SIEM.
[11:00] Mark: On performance: we want to run a benchmark that mirrors our 800 qps spike for 30 minutes and see latency tail behavior. Do you have a standard benchmarking harness?
[11:12] Samir: We do. We'll coordinate a canary run - typically we provision a dedicated cluster sized for your expected average and then we simulate the spike. We collect token-level latency, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, and we share an analysis spreadsheet.
[11:45] Aisha: How much engineering time should we budget for the pilot?
[11:52] Samir: Most customers allocate 2-3 engineers for 2-3 weeks for integrations (network, IAM, testing) and then one SRE/ops during handover. We provide runbooks and templates to reduce lift.
[12:20] Mark: Are there any constraints around model licensing if we bring our own weights?
[12:28] Laura: You manage your model licenses. We don't claim ownership; we host and serve them under the terms in the SLA. We'll surface any flags if models have special runtime requirements.
[13:00] Jing: What's your observability surface? We need token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, and traces correlated to logs.
[13:12] Samir: Redwood Console exposes per-route dashboards, token cost breakdowns, tracing hooks, and exportable logs. We can ship logs to your S3 or SIEM; retention is configurable.
[14:00] Aisha: Any known limitations: GPU types, unsupported ops, or frameworks?
[14:10] Samir: We support the common transformer ops; very custom kernels might need a port. GPU availability depends on region, but we can offer comparable instances. We'll check compatibility for your 70B pipeline.
[15:00] Mark: For the billing - do you meter tokens at request or generation time, and how do you handle retries and partial responses?
[15:12] Laura: Billing is per-token generation; partial responses count generated tokens. Retries are billed; we can set guardrails and circuit-breakers to avoid runaway retries.
[16:00] Aisha: For data residency, we need to ensure models and logs are stored in US region only. Is that doable?
[16:10] Samir: Yes - you can pin region for model storage and logs; we can disable cross-region backups for the Dedicated account.
[17:00] Jing: Network access - will we need to open ingress to Redwood?
[17:06] Samir: With Dedicated in your VPC, we use private networking; peering or Transit Gateway options. If you prefer an on-prem deploy, that's also possible.
[18:00] Mark: What about scaling down at night? We have predictable diurnal patterns and want to save cost.
[18:10] Samir: Autoscaling policies can scale pools down with min capacities for latency-sensitive routes. For very aggressive night downsizing, we recommend warm standby nodes for critical routes.
[19:00] Aisha: Are there any SLA numbers you can share?
[19:06] Laura: Our Dedicated SLA covers uptime with credits for downtime; we'll include specifics in the proposal.
[20:00] Mark: Any references - customers in fintech you can share?
[20:10] Laura: We have a couple of anonymized case studies (banks and payments) that show latency and cost improvements; I'll include links.
[21:00] Jing: Could you run a quick sketch of an architecture for us - dedicated cluster in VPC, KMS, SIEM integration, and fallback to hosted for non-sensitive routes?
[21:12] Samir: (brief verbal sketch) - you basically have reserved GPU nodes in your VPC, a control plane endpoint (can be private), KMS for keys, an egress policy that restricts fallback to hosted only for specific service routes, and logging exported to your SIEM. I'll send a diagram.
[23:00] Mark: Any pitfalls to watch for during the pilot?
[23:10] Samir: Watch sequence-length distribution - long tails can bottleneck inference. Also, model cache warming matters - if you roll hot models frequently you'll see cold-start overhead. We recommend warm pools for models with production traffic.
[25:00] Aisha: Decision timeline - we're aiming to decide by mid-April, budget cycle. Pilot late March / early April ideally.
[25:12] Laura: That aligns with our typical cadence - we'll target the benchmarking week of 2026-03-29.
[26:00] Mark: Any legal/contract constraints we should flag now? Data processing addendum, custom indemnities?
[26:10] Laura: Standard DPA and security addendum are included; for custom indemnities we can loop legal. I'll have our contracts SME flagged.
[28:00] Jing: One more: model versioning and rollback - if a rollout degrades quality what's the rollback path?
[28:12] Samir: We support model version pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to previous versions. Console shows per-model quality metrics if you push evals.
[30:00] Aisha: Great. Can you recap what you'll send after the call?
[30:10] Laura: Sure - pricing draft, SOC2 docs, architecture diagram, benchmark scheduling invite, and a sample benchmark spreadsheet.
[30:30] Mark: Perfect. Any final concerns from our side?
[30:40] Jing: We'll need an internal security review but so far sounds feasible.
[31:00] Aisha: Agreed.
[31:10] Samir: Quick note on the benchmark: if you can share the prompt set and token distribution it makes results meaningful.
[31:30] Mark: We'll extract a 30-minute representative sample and the 30-minute peak window.
[32:00] Laura: Great - we'll provision a canary slot and send details.
[33:00] (brief chitchat, laughter)
[36:00] Aisha: One last question on RBAC - we want to limit access to model deploy and billing.
[36:12] Samir: Console RBAC supports role groups and SSO via SAML/SCIM. You can map billing to finance group and limit deployments to ML engineers.
[38:00] Mark: About observability retention - we might want 1 year of traces for audits. Is that an add-on?
[38:10] Laura: We have retention tiers as add-ons. We'll call out pricing.
[40:00] Jing: Any network egress costs to consider on your side?
[40:08] Samir: Egress is typically billed separately if you send logs cross-region; otherwise it's within the region. We'll show a cost breakdown.
[42:00] Mark: Okay, sounds good.
[42:12] Aisha: Thanks all. Looking forward to receiving docs.
[52:00] (closing formalities)
[57:50] Laura: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the items discussed.
---
